en: Making the Chinese crack and crash,
When I was beating them,
Why did I not die then?
Looming like Ala-Too,
When I was resplendent,
Going to holy war and clashing,
The Muslims' golden banner—
When I held it,
Those who roused my wrath—
When I held them captive,
Those who truly angered me—
When I beat them,
When my strength was great,
When my blue-maned wolf was alive,
Why did I not die then?!
Zulpukor from my wrist—
In the days when I hung it there,
The eighteen thousand worlds—
In the days when I ruled them,
Havoc upon the face of the earth—
In the days when I brought it,
Six thousand otter pelts, a thousand silver ingots,
Crushing them, for my tribute,
In the days when I took it,
Across the face of the earth like a falcon—
In the days when I swept,
A piercing battle cry at the unbelievers—
In the days when I hurled it,
Why did I not die then?
I have herded camels in disgrace.
My lord Manas, take me with you!”
So saying, Khan Bakay then
Turned Kokcholok's head.
Speaking of his sorrow, brave Bakay
Now stood bellowing and weeping.
Speaking of his loss, mighty Bakay
Grieved most bitterly.
Wanting to die, but unable to die,
Unable to take his own life,
Taking a hare's paw in his hand,
Khan Bakay was no longer himself.
Hill upon hill, a little hill—
He stopped on a little hill.
Those ownerless beasts before him—
He looked for the missing ownerless beasts.
That one a young camel, that a fifth-year female,
That one a gelded camel, a young male,
As he looked over the mature camels,
Bakay suffered once again.
Now he turned Kokcholok's head;
As though his people had fallen into ruin,
Bakay stood bellowing now:
“Perish, you and your feast!
Why did I turn toward their feast?!
Let me eat a bullet instead of feast food!
I have lost my camels.
Perish, you and your funeral feast!
Why did I turn toward that feast?
Let me eat stones instead of food!
It was a beast left by Manas;
I have lost Zhelmayyan!
Its gray male companion is missing,
The gray female is missing with it,
Zhelmayyan is missing too.
Parted from Zhelmayyan,
White-bearded Bakay has no fortune!
You cursed, dim eyes,
Have you been gouged out?
You beard fit to be burned,
Have you been shorn today?
Good heavens, when the orphan comes tomorrow,
When he asks, ‘Where is Zhelmayyan?’
What torment shall I bear?
You beard fit to be shorn,
What answer shall I give?
What shall I do about that suffering?
With a golden halter on its head,
Bringing on misfortune like this,
My dear child Kanykey
Left it in my keeping!”
He turned Kokcholok's head;
Then he stood mourning Zhelmayyan's absence.
Semetey, riding Aktulpar,
When he saw Bakay,
The dear hero now decided to test him.
“My mother Kanykey said this:
‘Than my father Manas,
Bakay is the greater warrior,’ she said.
Let me speak in a different way;
Let me learn the secret within him.
If he is a lion greater than my father,
Let me take him as my shelter.
If he is a worthless old man,
Without making the poor fellow suffer much,
Let me sacrifice him now.
Concealing my own secret,
To Bakay standing here,
Let me go as a stranger.”
So saying, Semetey
It was separated from the moon,
He meant to go up to Bakay,
Close beside him as he watched.
Now he turned Aktulpar's head;
Then he gave his greeting.
The accomplished hero, the poor orphan,
Came up now and greeted him.
Your elder with seven spiritual patrons
He now tested thoroughly:
“Greetings and peace be upon you, brother-in-law!”
Then Bakay said this:
“And upon you be peace, my child.
What is your battle cry, what is your identity?
What is your clan, what is your village?
From which clan do you come?
There are twelve Muslim tribes,
Hindustan, whose tongue we do not know,
And twelve Kyrgyz tribes.
My child, from which clan do you come?
What is your lineage, what is your identity?
My child, which village did you come from?
My child, where was your umbilical cord cut?
My child, among what people did you grow up?”
Then the boy said this,
Without faltering, spoke the truth:
“Ah, brother-in-law, I am God's beloved servant.
I am a son of Janaaly and Karach from below,
Whom mortals who saw him called a hero,
Dwelling in Chambyl-Bel down below.
Why do you ask about my land?
Brother-in-law, do you think we have no land?
Why do you ask about my people?
Do you think I am a man without a people?
Brother-in-law, you once wrought havoc;
I have something to say.
When your Magnanimous Manas lived,
You once raided my village.
For that reason, khan brother-in-law,
I have vengeance to exact from you.
When your Magnanimous Manas lived,
Driving white deer and making cattle of them,
Throwing the places you fought into confusion,
When you brought humiliation on Kokand,
When you raided Margilan,
You raided Afghanistan, taking gold coins,
Taking a thousand black-eyed ones,
Loading elephants, taking gold coins.
In Chambyl-Bel, on my father—Janaaly, Karach—
Bringing fury no person had seen,
You and your Khan Manas
Brought a bloody slaughter.
Destroying and beating my father,
You seized my elder sister Korpoyan.
Thus you were steeped in plunder;
You made her a captive wife.
You plundered the spoils;
Thus you wrought havoc.
I was born of Karach;
Brother-in-law, I grew up and became a man.
Now take note, brother-in-law:
I have become the equal of a warrior's son.
To the words I have spoken,
Will you agree, brother-in-law?
Kokcholok beneath you,
As a gift to me now,
Will you give it, brother-in-law?
Your valor reached us
When you seized my elder sister.
Your torment went too far.
Taking a girl as great as a mountain,
Giving no bay-piebald yearling pacer,
Giving no whole joint of meat,
Your leaving us despondent was a humiliation!
When Magnanimous Manas lived,
You slaughtered my village.
This deed of yours was an outrage!
To what I have said for now,
Will you agree, brother-in-law?
I have come now: Kokcholok,
As compensation, you yourself—
Will you give it, brother-in-law?”
Now he spoke directly,
Now he stood as Bakay's enemy.
Leopard Bakay, the heroic lion,
Now spoke out with a shout:
“I agree, my child, I agree.
Kokcholok is yours to sacrifice.
His eyes had grown inflamed,
Let me give this along with her.
My child, what you said is indeed true;
Everything you said is true.
When my accomplished Manas was alive,
I swept across the face of the earth.
To that land of yours, Chambyl-Bel,
To your people of Sultan Kor-uulu,
These very hands of mine fought;
This very mouth of mine argued.
Your people with their great fur caps, bare chests,
And hoe-shaped rumps—
Four times I brought grief upon them.
Smashing your horses at the tethering rail,
Making their girls and young wives weep,
Making their women wail,
Not once, but your father
I raided six times.
I beat out your fury as one beats a sheep;
Thus I raided your father.
Your people who answered back,
My child, I sacrificed them.
Your elder sister Korpoyan,
I seized without giving livestock.
Your elder sister Korpoyan,
I put behind me on my horse.
My child, if your honor is stirred, be strong.
Your elder sister Korpoyan,
Thus I seized her.
I brought death upon his people;
Your elder sister Korpoyan,
I made my wife without a marriage rite.
I beat and slaughtered your khojas;
Your elder sister Korpoyan,
I made a captive wife.
I agree, my child, I agree.
Kokcholok beneath me,
Let me give it as a reward for good news.
I agree, my child, I agree.
Most of the old man’s life was gone;
My child, let me give it as bride-price.
Kokcholok is yours to sacrifice.
My child, I have blunted my steel;
Today I lost Zhelmayyan.
My wings have been broken;
Today I parted from Zhelmayyan.
There are no tracks where it walked on the earth,
Nor anyone who interfered with it.
It was a famed and mighty creature,
A beast left by my valiant Manas.
Counting its years of maturity,
Alas, it had reached ninety-five.
This very year Zhelmayyan
Was in its ninety-ninth year.
No wind could match its trot;
It was a beast like the unseen wind.
To seven spiritual masters he had pledged himself;
Alas, my Manas left it behind.
No beast could match its walk;
It was as swift as the wind.
My dark, blue-maned leopard,
Alas, my Manas left it behind.
Its swiftness was known to the people;
An inheritance left by my sun,
My child, its front lip was floppy,
Its rear hump flapped,
On its head was a golden halter:
Zhelmayyan, left by my Khan Manas.
When he journeyed to Mecca,
When he passed through Medina,
